title: Peak of banded iron formation deposition

facts.text: Massive banded iron formations precipitated across most continents.
Most of the world's banded iron deposits were laid down around 2.5 Ga, when deposition peaked.
Oxidized iron forms their red layers; the Siderian period takes its name from the Greek for iron.
Deposition began on the Kaapvaal and Pilbara cratons; Australia's Brockman Supersequence (2500–2449 Ma) holds iron-formation sediments laid down as seas rose.
The Hamersley Range BIFs, laid down 2470–2450 Ma, are the world's thickest and most extensive, over 900 m thick.

conflicts.note: History of Earth: abundant through the Siderian
Banded iron formation (own article): most deposits date to the late Archean

title: Mineral diversity explodes after the Great Oxidation

facts.text: The Great Oxygenation Event set off explosive growth in mineral diversity as many elements took oxidized forms near Earth's surface.
About 2,500 new minerals formed in the 2.5–1.9 Ga oxygenation stage, lifting the total above 4,000.
Oxidized uraninite alone gave over 200 new uranyl minerals; more than two-thirds of all mineral species owe their existence to life.

title: Breakup of Kenorland

facts.text: Magma-plume rifting began between 2.48 and 2.45 Ga in a supercontinent that had sat at low latitudes.
The drawn-out breakup left mafic dikes, rift basins and rifted margins on many continents through the Siderian and Rhyacian.
Final breakup produced large swarms of mafic dikes and sills across the North American provinces 2.2–2.1 Ga.
Its fragments became proto-continents including Laurentia, Baltica, the Yilgarn craton and Kalahari; the breakup is associated with the Paleoproterozoic glacial epoch.
In the alternative view, the Sclavia supercraton broke up during a global pulse of mantle-plume magmatism around 2.33–2.1 Ga.

contested_note: Kenorland itself is hypothetical; the continents may instead have formed two supercratons, Superia and Sclavia.

facts.text: About 2470 Ma the Mistassini dike swarm, itself a large igneous province over 100,000 km², cut the Superior Craton.
The related Matachewan dike swarm followed, covering at least 300,000 km² between Lake Superior and James Bay.
These intrusions are interpreted as hotspot-driven rifting near Sudbury, Ontario, at the onset of Kenorland's breakup.

facts.text: Free oxygen first built up in the air and shallow seas, turning a weakly reducing atmosphere into an oxidizing one, an irreversible change.
Cyanobacteria, the first known oxygen producers, are generally credited; oxygen won out once surface reductants such as ferrous iron, sulfur and methane were used up.
Oxygen rose from almost none to as much as 10% of the modern level by the end of the event.
Between 2410 and 2320 Ma the oxygen partial pressure rose from about two millionths of a bar to at least two thousandths.
Sulfur isotope anomalies typical of an oxygen-free sky vanish after 2.4–2.3 Ga, and rust-red beds appear in soils by 2.3 Ga.

facts.text: Free oxygen was toxic to the mostly anaerobic biosphere and may have wiped out many early organisms, mostly archaeal colonies.
It is described as the first known mass extinction, killing most of the planet's obligate anaerobes.
It may have been the worst ever, but early life is too poorly known to compare it with the Big Five.
It is the only well-documented extinction before the Phanerozoic, since earlier life was microbial or soft-bodied.

facts.text: Microfossils in black chert of Australia's Turee Creek Group date to 2450 Ma and are among the oldest known.
Carbonaceous microfossils from the group have been interpreted as iron-oxidizing bacteria.
The group's Kazput Reef Complex, dated 2400–2300 Ma, is the oldest known Proterozoic reef complex.

title: Sleaford orogeny forms the Gawler Craton

facts.text: The Sleaford orogeny deformed the Gawler craton of South Australia from 2440 to 2420 Ma.
The Gawler craton of Australia formed about 2,440 Ma.
Before 1550 Ma the craton was a set of active orogenic belts reaching back to at least 2450 Ma.
An impact struck the Bundelkhand craton, leaving the largest impact structure in India.
Its diameter is estimated at 3 km by some sources and 11 km by others, and its age is poorly constrained.
The Dhala impact is estimated to have occurred between 2.44 and 2.24 Ga.
The Scourie dike swarm cut Scotland's Lewisian gneisses, overlapping the Inverian deformation at the start of the Proterozoic.
Around 2410 Ma the Widgiemooltha swarm intruded the Yilgarn Craton, close in time to the Sebanga Poort dike in Zimbabwe.
Dike swarms and volcanic intrusions appeared in plates of Northwestern Europe, South Africa and Australia in connection with the rifting of Kenorland.
Despite the dike intrusions contributing to rifting, Kenorland experienced little continental movement and there are no signs of ocean development.
Filaments that grew inside cracks and gas cavities of basalt in South Africa's Ongeluk Formation have been suggested to be fossils of fungi-like organisms.
They are the earliest fossils with features typical of fungi: bottom-dwelling, multicellular, with filaments able to fuse together.
Ukraine's much younger Volyn biota is cited as further support for their fungal nature.

verification.title: Fungus-like mycelial fossils in 2.4-billion-year-old vesicular basalt

facts.text: A series of glacial periods, also called the Makganyene glaciation, named for diamictite-bearing rocks of the Huronian Supergroup near Lake Huron.
Rising oxygen cut atmospheric methane from 300 to 4 ppmv, weakening the greenhouse; average global temperatures fell below 0 °C.
The Siderian page dates three pulses: about 2440–2420 Ma (Duitschland), 2380–2360 Ma (Makganyene) and 2340–2310 Ma (Gowganda/Rietfontein).
Glacial deposits occur on six cratons, including Wyoming, Kaapvaal and Karelia-Kola, and correlate with Western Australian beds.
It is the earliest well-established ice age, with land-based ice; only the Pongola glaciation is older.

facts.text: The Makganyene glaciation of South Africa has been proposed as a 'snowball Earth' triggered by the evolution of cyanobacteria.
Its glacial sediments, slightly younger than the Huronian deposits, were possibly laid down at tropical latitudes.
Paleomagnetic evidence places South African glacial deposits of 2.2 Ga near the equator.
Cap carbonates sit above its glacial beds.

facts.text: Marine carbonates record the largest and longest-lasting positive carbon isotope excursion known, with δ13C values of +5 to +30‰.
Matching it would have needed the burial of organic carbon to double or triple for millions of years.
It accompanied a massive rise in atmospheric oxygen, an expansion of life and more burial of organic matter.
Oxygen climbed around 2.3 Ga, then fell around 2.1 Ga in the Shunga-Francevillian event, letting organic-rich black shales accumulate.
If it was globally synchronous, it lasted between about 128 and 249 million years.

title: Yarrabubba impact

facts.text: An impactor about 7 km wide struck the Yilgarn craton of Western Australia, leaving a crater 30–70 km across.
Its date falls near the end of the Huronian glaciation, and simulations fit an impact into a 2-km-thick ice sheet.
Zircon and monazite dating made it the oldest impact structure of confident age until 2025, when Miralga displaced it; a later study challenged its date.

contested_note: A later study challenged the 2.229 Ga date and suggested a much younger impact.

verification.title: Precise radiometric age establishes Yarrabubba, Western Australia, as Earth’s oldest recognised meteorite impact structure

facts.text: A series of tectonic, metamorphic and plutonic events reshaped what is now West Africa.
It built the Eglab and Man shields of the West African Craton and structured its Birimian domain.
With the Transamazonian orogen it welded South American and West African cratons during Columbia's assembly.
Around 2070 Ma an upwelling of the asthenosphere released a large volume of post-orogenic magma.
Continental red beds formed as iron in weathered sandstone was exposed to oxygen.
Hematite-coloured red beds signal rising atmospheric oxygen; the first were laid down in the Rhyacian.
Iron in ancient soils shows oxygen reaching 5–18% of present levels around 2,200 Ma.

title: First eukaryotes

facts.text: Eukaryotes are thought to have arisen in the Rhyacian when an Asgard archaeon took in an alphaproteobacterium; sexual reproduction probably appeared then too.
The earliest known eukaryotic acritarchs, organic-walled microfossils, date from between 2150 and 1950 Ma.
Another view puts the earliest evidence at 1.85 Ga, from symbiogenesis between archaea and proteobacteria under new oxidative stress.
Claimed eukaryote records from 2.1 Ga are considered questionable; the oldest unambiguous eukaryote remains, from China, are 1.8–1.6 Ga old.

contested_note: When eukaryotes first appeared is debated; claimed fossils from around 2.1 Ga are considered questionable.

facts.text: Two small Archean proto-continents, the Gavião and Jequié blocks, collided.
It shaped what are now the São Francisco Craton and the Guiana Shield.
With West Africa's Eburnean orogen, it marks the start of Columbia's assembly.

title: Francevillian biota

facts.text: Black shales of Gabon's Francevillian B Formation hold flattened, disk-shaped structures up to 17 cm across.
Some authors read them as the earliest multicellular life and the earliest eukaryotes.
A 2017 review called their biological origin questionable; a 2023 review suggested they may be artifacts of diagenesis.
A 2023 isotope study found light-zinc enrichment that could reflect eukaryotic metabolism.

contested_note: Whether the structures are fossils at all is disputed; recent reviews lean towards a non-biological origin.

facts.text: Global-scale collisions gathered almost all of Earth's continental blocks into the supercontinent Columbia, also called Nuna.
Its proto-cratons became the cores of Laurentia, Baltica, the Ukrainian Shield, Amazonia and Australia, possibly with Siberia, North China and Kalaharia.
The collisions included the Trans-Hudson, Limpopo, Capricorn and Trans-North China orogenies.
Zircons record an extensive high mountain range, the Nuna Supermountains, at 2.0–1.8 Ga.
Modern plate tectonics may have emerged by at least 2.2 Ga with Columbia's formation.

title: Shungite: Karelian lagoon muds become petroleum

facts.text: Organic-rich muds settled in a brackish lagoon in Russian Karelia during active rifting; volcanic nutrients may have raised biological productivity.
The sequence is dated by a 1980 ± 27 Ma gabbro intrusion and underlying dolomites of 2090 ± 70 Ma; the deposit holds over 250 gigatonnes of carbon.
Metamorphism turned these oil source rocks into shungite; its veins and layers are migrated petroleum, now bitumen, of confirmed biological origin.
Mantle magma rose through long cracks in the Kaapvaal crust, forming the largest layered igneous intrusion in Earth's crust.
It holds the world's largest reserves of platinum-group metals, plus vast amounts of iron, tin, chromium, titanium and vanadium.
Layered like a cake, it includes three platinum-bearing layers called reefs.
The intrusion predates the nearby Vredefort impact by about 30 million years.

facts.text: An asteroid struck the Kaapvaal craton in today's South Africa; first put at 10–15 km wide, it was estimated at 20–25 km in 2022.
It left the largest verified impact structure on Earth; the original crater was 170–300 km across, possibly larger than Chicxulub.
Erosion of 7–11 km has removed the crater; the Vredefort Dome's 70 km ring of hills is its rebounded central uplift.
It was one of two of the largest known impacts of the Orosirian.
By dropping the Witwatersrand rocks down, the strike preserved rich gold deposits that would otherwise have been eroded away.

title: Glenburgh orogeny joins Pilbara and Yilgarn

facts.text: The Pilbara Craton and the Glenburgh Terrane collided with the Yilgarn craton in Western Australia.
It brought substantial granite magmatism and intense deformation and metamorphism to the Glenburgh Terrane.
The Glenburgh Terrane's collision with the Yilgarn craton created the Errabiddy Shear Zone.
Between 1990 and 2004 some geologists proposed that the orogeny resulted from the collision of the Yilgarn and Pilbara cratons.
Cratons now in West Africa and eastern South America joined to form the continent Atlantica.
It included Amazonia and the Congo, West Africa and North Africa cratons.
It is not generally regarded as a supercontinent.

verification.title: A History of Continents in the past Three Billion Years

facts.text: Mountain building affected what are now Sweden, Finland and Russia, joining cratons of Baltica within Columbia.
Subduction closed an ocean basin and emplaced the Jormua and Outokumpu ophiolites about 1950 Ma.
Continent–continent collision lasted from 1870 to 1790 Ma, overlapping with extension in the south.
The orogen then collapsed under gravity from 1790 to 1770 Ma.
The largest Paleoproterozoic orogenic belt in the world, it formed the Canadian Shield and the North American craton, Laurentia.
It sutured the Hearne-Rae, Superior and Wyoming cratons into North America's cratonic core.
Old cratonic blocks, island arcs and ocean deposits were folded, thrust, metamorphosed and intruded by hundreds of huge granite bodies.
It was the culminating event of Laurentia's assembly from six or seven Archean fragments, following the Wopmay orogeny.
Final closure of the Manikewan Ocean around 1.83 Ga merged the Hearne, Superior and Sask cratons; metamorphism peaked about 1.82–1.8 Ga.
Baltica formed from the collision of three blocks: Fennoscandia, Sarmatia and Volgo-Uralia.
Sarmatia and Volgo-Uralia joined as Proto-Baltica at c. 2.0 Ga, then collided with Fennoscandia c. 1.8–1.7 Ga.
Sarmatia and Fennoscandia collided c. 1.84–1.82 Ga after a calm period following subduction.
Mountain building that was a key event in the assembly of Antarctica.
It joined East Antarctica to an unknown continental block as Columbia formed.
Much of central Antarctica was added to the nucleus of the continent in East Antarctica during this orogeny.
Many of the rocks were deformed and metamorphosed close to the end of the orogeny, around 1.7 billion years ago.
Mountain building affected Greenland, forming the northern boundary of the mainly Archean North Atlantic craton.
Island-arc terranes and two possible sutures within the belt record vanished subduction zones.
It was one of the orogens that sutured Laurentia's cratonic blocks within Columbia.
Widespread mafic–ultramafic magmatism built the Circum-Superior Belt, a large igneous province, along the Superior craton's margin 1,884–1,870 Ma.
Its dikes, sills and lavas stretch over 3,400 km from Manitoba to Labrador and were emplaced in an extremely short geological time span.
It erupted while the Trans-Hudson, New Quebec and Penokean orogenies surrounded the Superior craton; in the Labrador Trough its 1,880 Ma magmatic event covered about 30,000 km².
Its origin is unclear: proposals include back-arc rifting, foredeep flexure, mantle plumes and microcontinent breakup; a 1,900 Ma global superplume is questioned.
It hosts major copper, nickel and platinum-group deposits, including Manitoba's Thompson nickel belt, and a rare Proterozoic komatiite belt.

facts.text: The Hottah terrane, a continental magmatic arc, collided with the Archean Slave Craton in northern Canada, closing the Coronation Ocean between them.
The belt is about 500 km long and 200 km wide; Great Bear arc magmatism continued until about 1.84 Ga.
Its oceanic crust, island arcs and colliding continents show that modern plate-tectonic forces were at work in the early Proterozoic.
Black chert layers in banded iron formation on Lake Superior's north shore preserve microfossils of microbes like cyanobacteria.
The rock is built of biogenic stromatolites; some cyanobacterial colonies in Ontario have turned to jasper.
The microbiota shows photosynthesis was under way and the atmosphere held enough oxygen to sustain microbial life.
Uranium–lead dating gives a consensus age of about 1.878 Ga; interbedded ash layers date to 1.86–1.99 Ga.

title: Grypania: possible early eukaryote

facts.text: Grypania is a coiled, tube-shaped fossil over a centimetre long, one of the most common large Proterozoic fossils.
The oldest probable specimens date to about 1870 Ma, redated from 2100 Ma; the genus lasted into the Ediacaran.
If it was an alga, eukaryotes with organelles had already evolved.

contested_note: Its identity is uncertain: it could have been a giant bacterium, a bacterial colony or a eukaryotic alga.

facts.text: Mountain building struck the Lake Superior region, in an embayment on the southern margin of the Superior Craton.
A collision between two domains drove northward thrusting and folding, and reactivated the Great Lakes tectonic zone.
It was one of the 1.9–1.8 Ga orogens that sutured Laurentia's cratonic blocks during Columbia's assembly.
Bacterial viruses (bacteriophages) emerged before, or soon after, the prokaryotic and eukaryotic lineages diverged.

facts.text: Banded iron formations largely vanish from the rock record worldwide after 1.85 Ga.
Their end is read as the oxygenation of the deep ocean, once the iron dissolved in seawater had been oxidized.
Before then the ocean was persistently iron-rich, with possible intervals of sulfidic euxinia.
The only extensive iron formations laid down later are tied to Cryogenian glacial deposits.
A 10 km asteroid struck water about 1,000 m deep 1.849 Ga, at the same time as a pause in iron-formation deposition.

title: Trans-North China Orogen unites the North China Craton

facts.text: The Eastern and Western Blocks of the North China Craton collided over an eastward-dipping subduction zone, forming the Trans-North China Orogen; Zhao ties this to Columbia's assembly.
Kusky instead dates the amalgamation to 2.5–2.3 Ga and reads the 1.85 Ga event as a collision with Columbia.
Earlier, about 1.95 Ga, the Yinshan and Ordos blocks collided to form the Western Block and the Khondalite Belt.

contested_note: The timing of the craton's amalgamation is disputed between a 2.5 Ga model (Kusky) and a 1.85 Ga model (Zhao).

facts.text: A chondritic bolide 10–15 km wide struck the Nuna supercontinent in what is now Ontario, Canada.
It left one of the oldest and largest known impact structures; debris would have been scattered across the globe.
The Sudbury Igneous Complex formed at the same time; its ores hold nickel, copper, platinum-group metals, gold and silver.
It has been proposed that the impact mixed the stratified ocean through tsunamis, vaporized seawater and runoff from wrecked continental margins.
It was one of the two largest known impacts of the Orosirian, near the end of the period.

facts.text: It followed the collision of the Pilbara Craton and Glenburgh Terrane with the Yilgarn craton in Western Australia.
It was the most important and widespread of the four orogenies that shaped the Gascoyne Complex, marked by intracratonic reworking.
Voluminous Moorarie granites intruded the complex, and flood basalts erupted in the Yerrida Basin around 1830 Ma.
After final assembly at c. 1.82 Ga, Columbia kept growing until 1.5 Ga through subduction-related magmatism and accretion at its margins.
A great magmatic belt formed along what are now the southern margins of North America, Greenland and Baltica.
Similar accretionary belts grew around Amazonia, the North Australia and Gawler cratons, and North China.
Extensive magmatism about 1,750 Ma in Baltica, Sarmatia, Siberia, Laurentia and West Africa shows these cratons were linked.

facts.text: The oldest ergs, or sand seas, developed on several cratons.
An informal span from about 1.8 to 0.8 billion years ago, also called Earth's Middle Ages, marked by tectonic stability, climatic stasis and slow biological evolution.
Bracketed by oxygenation events and global glaciations, it had very low oxygen and no glaciations, though a 1 Ga Scottish lake froze over in winter.
Its oceans may have been oxygen-poor, sulfidic and nutrient-starved, dominated by purple bacteria that used hydrogen sulfide instead of water: a so-called Canfield ocean.
The carbon isotope record shows no major excursions, and Mesoproterozoic global temperatures may have averaged about 19 °C, some 4 °C warmer than today.
It ended with the breakup of Rodinia in the Tonian, a second oxygenation event and the Cryogenian Snowball Earth.

facts.text: The Yavapai island arc terrane collided with proto-North America in what is now New Mexico and Arizona.
It was one of several arc terranes accreted onto Laurentia's 1800 Ma core; related events include the Colorado and Central Plains orogenies.
The Grand Canyon's Vishnu basement schists formed 1.75–1.73 Ga as island arcs collided with the mainland.

facts.text: Natural nuclear fission reactors were generating power in what is now Oklo, Gabon.
Concentrated uranium deposits started reacting after groundwater flooded them; the reactions ran on and off, probably never above 100 kilowatts.
The existence of the Oklo reactors was confirmed through analysis of isotope ratios of uranium and of the fission products and their stable daughter nuclides.
Groundwater-moderated natural reactors are not thought to have been possible before the early photosynthesizers began producing oxygen on a planetary scale.

facts.text: The Mazatzal island arc terrane collided with proto-North America in what is now New Mexico and Arizona.
It followed the Yavapai orogeny as the next pulse in the growth of southern Laurentia.
Short-lived extensional basins between the two orogenies filled with quartzite and rhyolite.

facts.text: The Chuanlinggou Formation of the Yan Mountains, North China, preserves the first definitive multicellular eukaryotes: Qingshania, Tawuia and Changchengia.
Multicellular organisms with differentiated cells performing specialized functions began to appear around 1.7 Ga.
Qingshania, dated elsewhere to 1.7 Ga, appears to consist of nearly identical cells.
Multicellular eukaryotes, likely descended from colonies of single cells, probably evolved about 2–1.4 Ga.
Such finds show that Mesoproterozoic life was not purely microbial, as once thought.

title: Shoemaker impact

facts.text: An impact in the Mid West of Western Australia left a structure with shatter cones and shocked quartz, at least 30 km across.
Its most cited age, about 1,630 Ma, records a reheating of the granite that may be the impact or only a regional tectonic event.
More recent K-Ar dating gives ages as young as 568 ± 20 Ma, which could date the impact or represent tectonic activity.
The first suggestion that the ring-like topographic feature may be an impact structure was published in 1974.

contested_note: The impact age is uncertain: the 1,630 Ma date may record a tectonic reheating rather than the impact.

conflicts.note: K-Ar ages as young as this could also date the impact or tectonic activity

facts.text: The Chitrakoot Formation in India's Vindhya Range preserves the earliest known red algae, Rafatazmia and Ramathallus.
The oldest known red algal mats date to about 1.6 Ga.
Rafatazmia chitrakootensis is a filamentous alga described from dolomite from the Vindhya Ranges of central India.
Its cells have been said to be similar to oscillatoriacean cyanobacteria and probably multicellular red algae.
The find pushes back the age of the oldest red alga by about 400 million years, to about 1,650 ± 89 (2σ) million years ago.

verification.title: Three-dimensional preservation of cellular and subcellular structures suggests 1.6 billion-year-old crown-group red algae

title: Isan orogeny and the Mount Isa ore deposits

facts.text: The Isan orogeny, a major mountain-building event, affected Queensland's Mount Isa Block about 1,600 Ma as large lead, silver, copper and zinc deposits were laid down.
Mount Isa's lower lead–zinc–silver ore and upper copper ore lie in the 1,000 m thick Lower Proterozoic Urquhart Shale, on one limb of a faulted fold.
The Mount Isa belt is one of the 1.8–1.5 Ga magmatic belts that grew along the North Australia Craton's margins.
Around 1.6 Ga some eukaryotes took up cyanobacteria as endosymbionts, gaining oxygenic photosynthesis through plastids.
These became the algae, which eventually overtook cyanobacteria as the dominant primary producers.
The Gaoyuzhuang Formation of North China, about 1,589 Ma, preserves some of the first algae, such as Tuanshanzia and Grandilingulata.
A diverse collection of fossil algae occurs in rocks dated between 1.5 and 1.4 Ga.

conflicts.note: History of life section dates the plastid symbiosis to about 1.5 Ga

verification.title: A molecular timescale of eukaryote evolution and the rise of complex multicellular life

facts.text: Oxygen is proposed to have risen transiently to about 4% of present levels at times between 1.59 and 1.36 Ga.
Gaoyuzhuang rocks suggest a rise near 1.57 Ga; formations in Australia, Russia and North China show oxygenation near 1.4 Ga, though how global is unclear.
The seafloor was about 50–80% oxidized early in the Ectasian, declining afterwards.
Otherwise Boring Billion oxygen may have stayed below 0.1–1% of modern levels, stalling complex life.

verification.title: An expansive global oxygenation of Earth’s surface environments 1.4 billion years ago

facts.text: Exceptionally preserved microfossils formed in cavities of igneous rocks in what is now Zhytomyr Oblast, Ukraine, about 1.5 Ga.
They include filaments of varied shapes and fungus-like organisms, possibly among the first fossils of the deep biosphere.
Precambrian fossils are usually not well preserved, but the Volyn biota had exceptional conditions for fossilization in cavities with silicon tetrafluoride-rich fluids.
The Volyn samples were found in miarolitic pegmatites collected from the Korosten Pluton of the Ukrainian Shield.

facts.text: Columbia began to fragment about 1.5–1.35 Ga, with rifting along the margins of Laurentia, India, Baltica, Siberia, southern Africa and North China.
Widespread magmatism away from mountain belts formed anorthosite–mangerite–charnockite–granite suites in North America, Baltica, Amazonia and North China.
Atlantica split from Nena, and North China broke away along the Zhaertai–Bayan Obo rift, where mafic sills record the event.
Final breakup came about 1.3–1.2 Ga, marked by the 1.27 Ga Mackenzie and 1.24 Ga Sudbury dyke swarms in North America.
The fragments later reassembled into the supercontinent Rodinia.

title: Horodyskia, a 'string of beads' organism

facts.text: Horodyskia, a string of beads joined by a fine thread, is one of the oldest known eukaryotes; its fossils span 1,480 to 550 Ma.
It may have been an early animal, but has also been read as a colonial foraminiferan.
It ranks among the first structurally complex eukaryotes.

contested_note: Its identity is unsettled: sources read it as a possible early animal or as a colonial foraminiferan.

title: Belt Basin fills on Laurentia's western edge

facts.text: Much of the Belt Supergroup was laid down about 1450–1400 Ma in a fault-bounded rift basin on the edge of Laurentia, within the supercontinent Columbia.
Mostly fine mud, silt and sand piled up more than 15 km thick over some 200,000 km², in a basin that was probably closed or lake-like.
Its rocks hold stromatolites and rich lead, zinc and silver ores, and they form the mountains of Glacier National Park.

conflicts.note: Timeline of Earth lists the Belt Supergroup under its c. 1,600 Ma Calymmian entry

facts.text: A mountain-building event struck what is now the southwestern United States from 1.43 to 1.3 Ga.
Its batholiths of about 1,400 Ma make up over 20% of exposed Precambrian rock in New Mexico and the Rocky Mountains.
Much of the mid-continent is underlain by the 1,450–1,350 Ma Granite-Rhyolite crustal province.
A series of orogenic events in Africa ran from about 1,400 Ma until about 1,000 Ma, when Rodinia was assembled.
From 1.4 to 1.2 Ga it fused the Tanzanian and Congo cratons.
In a narrower sense, the name covers an event about 1,375 Ma that formed the Karagwe-Ankolean belt.

title: Large igneous province and Ectasian superplume

facts.text: A major large igneous province about 1,380 Ma links Laurentia, Baltica, Siberia, Congo and West Africa, formed as the Nuna supercontinent broke up.
Magmatism of the same age in Congo and Siberia shows the two continents stayed close for at least 120 million years.
Metamafic rocks of 1.37–1.35 Ga suggest a superplume affected three provinces, driving expansion and Columbia's breakup.
A massive igneous event starting about 1,270 Ma built a province of 2.7 million km² across the Canadian Shield, from Arctic Nunavut to the Great Lakes.
It includes the Muskox layered intrusion, the Coppermine River flood basalts and the huge Mackenzie dike swarm.
Its volume was about 3 million km³, linked to the Mackenzie hotspot.
Its dykes mark the final breakup of the supercontinent Columbia.

conflicts.note: Same page dates the dike swarm emplacement to about 1,200 Ma

facts.text: Fragments of the broken-up Columbia accreted and collided to form Rodinia, which assembled between 1.26 and 0.90 Ga.
Laurentia formed its core; it grew into the largest landmass yet, joining North American, East European, Amazonian, West African, Antarctic, Australian and Chinese blocks.
A global superocean, Mirovia, surrounded it; the proto-Pacific Panthalassa later grew at its expense.
Baltica and Amazonia collided with Laurentia in the 1.1–0.9 Ga Grenville, Sveconorwegian and Sunsás orogenies.
Its configuration and history are much less well understood than those of later supercontinents.

facts.text: Stromatolites, mounds built by microbial colonies, reached their greatest abundance and diversity about 1.25 Ga.
Widespread cyanobacterial colonies and reefs then dominated the tidal zones of oceans and seas.
After about 1,250 Ma their abundance and diversity declined steeply, perhaps as predators began grazing on stromatolites and acritarchs.
The decline sped up around 1 Ga, at the end of the Stenian; grazing by more complex organisms is the most widely supported explanation.
By the start of the Cambrian they had fallen to 20% of their peak; Proterozoic stromatolites preserve cyanobacteria and possibly green algae.

facts.text: A long-lived mountain-building event, tied to the assembly of Rodinia, raised a belt from Labrador to Mexico and on to Scotland.
Laurentia collided with other blocks, notably Amazonia, beginning the construction of what are now the Appalachian Mountains.
Its main pulses were the Elzevirian (1240–1220 Ma), Ottawan (1090–1020 Ma) and Rigolet (1010–980 Ma).
Crust of this age is found worldwide; the same events are called Kibaran in Africa, Dalslandian in western Europe and Sunsás in Brazil.
From about 1190 to 980 Ma two continental blocks collided with Laurentia, folding mountains from Newfoundland to North Carolina.
Between 1.22 and 1.12 Ga three orogenic events shaped the Musgrave Province of central Australia, a 220,000 km² region formed via a magma plume.
The Musgravian orogeny about 1,200 Ma generated the voluminous Kulgera granites by melting the lower crust.
The Musgrave event is interpreted as an intracontinental orogeny caused by significant upwelling of heat and material from the mantle.
The Musgrave Block is mainly exposed through the Petermann Orogeny at about 535-550 Ma, which exhumed the orogenic belt along the Woodroffe Thrust.

facts.text: The Stac Fada Member records an impact about 1.2 Ga; its inferred crater, about 40 km wide, has not been found.
The Stac Fada Member is an impactite made of a mixture of suevite and clast-poor impact melt rocks.
The Stac Fada Member is exposed along about 50 km of the Wester Ross coast, from the western side of Loch Ewe in the south to the Stoer peninsula in the north.
The member records an impact in the near vicinity, likely in the Minch or near Lairg.

facts.text: Nine formations of the Grand Canyon Supergroup were laid down in a sea between 1.2 billion and 740 million years ago, the Chuar Group in coastal and shallow seas.
Its oldest layer, averaging 1250 Ma, is the oldest in the canyon with fossils (stromatolites); the Cardenas Basalt, 1070 ± 70 Ma, tops the Unkar Group.
About 800 Ma the Grand Canyon orogeny tilted the supergroup 15° and broke it into fault blocks.

facts.text: A mountain-building system was active from 1140 to 960 Ma in what is now southwestern Sweden and southern Norway.
Its most active phase, 1050–980 Ma, metamorphosed and thickened the crust; a collision between Amazonia and Baltica may have caused it.
It is grouped with the Grenvillian orogens that assembled Rodinia.

facts.text: About 1.1 Ga the core of North America began to split apart, opening a rift 2,000 km long through the middle of the continent.
The rift failed, leaving thick layers of igneous rock; it is the deepest failed rift on Earth.
Lava poured from cracks along the rift valley; its arms meet at Lake Superior, which fills the valley.
Its western arm runs through Wisconsin, Minnesota, Iowa and Nebraska; the eastern arm reaches central Michigan.
Magmatism of about the same age struck Africa, India and South America.
An oxygenated lake in the Midcontinent Rift preserved freshwater microbes exceptionally well in what is now Michigan.
Its shale, siltstone and sandstone, 150–210 m thick, extend from Michigan and Wisconsin to Iowa.
The Nonesuch beds contain common organic carbon and pyrite.
The Nonesuch Shale has enough organic carbon (greater than 0.5%) to be a potential petroleum source bed, but exploration wells in Michigan, Wisconsin and Iowa found no commercial petroleum.

facts.text: In central Australia, the Warakurna large igneous province intruded the Giles Complex and Winburn granites and erupted the Bentley Supergroup volcanics.
A link to the 1110 Ma African-Indian-Amazonian event is possible but unlikely.
The Bentley Supergroup volcanics are bimodal volcanic rocks formed during the Warakurna Large Igneous Province and are widely considered comagmatic with the Giles Complex intrusions.
The Palgrave Volcanic Association is a large volcanic and granite caldera edifice of about 1500 square kilometres.
Bangiomorpha pubescens, a multicellular red alga from Somerset Island, Canada, closely resembles the living red alga Bangia.
Its differentiated reproductive cells are the oldest evidence of sexual reproduction and meiosis.
It is the earliest known organism that certainly had differentiated, specialized cells, and the oldest belonging to a living phylum.
Sex increased genetic variation, speeding evolution and the diversification of eukaryotes.

facts.text: Ourasphaira giraldae, multicellular organic-walled microfossils with fungal affinity, is preserved in shale of the Grassy Bay Formation, Canadian Arctic.
It is the earliest known fungus, dated 1.01–0.89 Ga.
Older fossils from 1.43 Ga have also been interpreted as multicellular fungi with differentiated cells.

facts.text: Eukaryotes, long inconspicuous, diversified rapidly around 1 Ga.
Acritarchs boomed in abundance, diversity, size and shape, growing more and longer spines, in their first large radiation.
The first dinoflagellates, some of which ate prey, may have been the first predators, pushing acritarchs into an arms race of defences.
After 1 Ga species durations dropped to about 100 million years, perhaps from increased grazing by early protists.

conflicts.note: Timeline of Earth: first dinoflagellates evolve c. 1,100 Ma

facts.text: Abundant eukaryotic microfossils from Scotland's freshwater Torridon Group suggest eukaryotes dominated non-marine habitats by 1 Ga.
Nutrients from continental runoff probably favoured them near the continents.
By then eukaryotes, including multicellular forms, inhabited freshwater environments.
Phosphatic microfossils from Scotland's Diabaig Formation, 994 ± 48 Ma, are among the oldest known non-marine eukaryotes.
Molecular-clock evidence suggests photosynthetic, multicellular eukaryotes and fungi had moved onto land by 1000 Ma.
Proterocladus antiquus, about 1 billion years old, is the first known preserved case of multicellularity in green algae.
Around 1 Ga the first multicellular plants emerged, probably green algae, though the line between a colony and a multicellular organism is blurred.
Proterocladus is a green alga known from the Nanfen and Diaoyutai Formations in China and the Svanbergfjellet Formation in Norway.
Cell size and septa constrictions vary in P. antiquus, casting doubt on every other Proterocladus species from the Svanbergfjellet Formation.
In lab studies of unicellular green algae, populations that grew into multicellular structures showed greater survival under predation.

facts.text: A mountain-building event, also called the Nimrod orogeny, struck Antarctica around 1 billion years ago.
It may have begun the Gamburtsev mountain range and the Vostok Subglacial Highlands.

title: Rayner orogeny: India collides with East Antarctica

facts.text: Proto-India and Antarctica collided in the Rayner orogeny, from about 1,000 Ma until about 900 Ma.
Rocks of East Antarctica's Rayner Complex and northern Prince Charles Mountains are an extension of India's Eastern Ghats.
They belong to a Grenville-age belt along East Antarctica's coast, read as a suture with southern Africa, India and western Australia, active until 900 Ma.

title: Bitter Springs microfossils

facts.text: Cherts of Australia's Bitter Springs Group preserve stromatolites and exceptionally well-preserved cyanobacteria in silica.
Some fossils with ghostly internal structures, such as Glenobotrydion, have been read as green algae, among the earliest plants.
This style of preservation ended in the late Neoproterozoic, when silica-secreting organisms appeared.

contested_note: The claim that the site preserves eukaryotic green algae is debated.

title: First putative animals (sponge-like fossils)

facts.text: Sponge-like fossils in reefs about 890 Ma may be the oldest animals, but their identity is highly debated.
The first putative animal fossils date to the middle to late Tonian, c. 890–800 Ma; Otavia, about 800 Ma, has been described as a primitive sponge.
Molecular studies place the base of the animal family tree in the Tonian, though physical evidence for such early animals is lacking.
Sponges, a basal animal group, emerged in the Tonian and survived the later glaciations.

contested_note: The identity of the earliest sponge-like fossils is highly debated, and physical evidence for Tonian animals is thin.

facts.text: From 870 Ma island arcs began building the Arabian-Nubian Shield as the Mozambique Ocean closed.
Arc collisions and terrane suturing followed at 780 Ma, with final assembly by 550 Ma.
Gold mined in antiquity in Egypt and Sudan comes almost entirely from its Neoproterozoic rocks.
Called the 'Second Great Oxidation Event', it raised oxygen in the air and oceans c. 850–540 Ma; marine rocks of 850–720 Ma record a large positive carbon-isotope excursion.
Oxygen rose from under 0.1% of present levels to over 13% during 900–815 Ma, and possibly to about 50% in the Cryogenian interglacial.
Oxygen rose above 1% of the atmosphere for the first time; air trapped in 813-million-year-old rock salt holds 10.9% oxygen.
It may have been one global event or a series of regional episodes, and the deep ocean stayed anoxic and iron-rich as late as 580 Ma.
The oxygen surge drove rapid evolution of multicellular life late in the era; some authors credit it with letting the oxygen-hungry Ediacaran biota spread.

facts.text: Macroscopic, small worm-shaped organisms near Huainan City, Anhui, China, record a transitional stage in evolution, 840–740 Ma.
A similar biota about 1 billion years old was found on Russia's Timan Ridge.
The Huainan biota organisms were discovered by Wang Guixiang and Sun Weiguo in the 1980s in Precambrian rock formations near Huainan City.
Huainan biota contain no jellyfish-like discs, as seen in the Ediacaran biota, and no forms close to sponges.
Deposition in the Adelaide Superbasin began just before 830 Ma as Laurentia started to rift away from Australia.
Its rift troughs and passive-margin basins kept developing until about 550 Ma.
Its rocks record Rodinia's breakup, two Snowball Earth glaciations, the Neoproterozoic oxygenation and the Ediacaran fauna.

facts.text: Around 800 Ma eukaryote fossils became notably more complex and numerous, as oceanic sulfide levels fell.
By about 750 Ma some small algae were mineralized, probably as armour against single-celled eukaryotic predators.
Yet persistent anoxia and euxinia kept overall eukaryotic diversity low through the late Tonian.

facts.text: Marine planktonic cyanobacteria first appeared about 800 Ma, descended from seafloor and freshwater ancestors, and helped oxygenate the oceans.
Planktonic nitrogen fixers that evolved in the Cryogenian ended a long shortage of ammonium that had held back multicellular life.
Their spread is thought to have sped oxygenation and carbon dioxide removal, helping explain the severe Cryogenian glaciations.
Rifting along the eastern margin of the West African craton during Rodinia's breakup opened the Pharusian Ocean about 800 Ma.
It began to close about 730 Ma as the Tilemsi arc was subducted eastward against the Hoggar region.
The western Hoggar massif is made of material from the Pharusian Ocean, including oceanic basalts, arc volcanic and sedimentary rocks.
The Trans-Saharan Belt, running from Algeria to Benin, marks the suture zone of the Pharusian Ocean closure.

title: East African Orogeny joins East and West Gondwana

facts.text: Gondwana began to form c. 800–650 Ma as India and Madagascar collided with East Africa in the East African Orogeny.
It was the main stage in joining East and West Gondwana along the Mozambique Belt, uniting Africa, India and Arabia.
The Arabian-Nubian Shield collided with eastern Africa in the Kenya–Tanzania region.
The Mozambique Ocean between Madagascar–India and the Congo–Tanzania craton began closing between 700 and 580 Ma.
In one model, arc accretion became a continental collision when Azania struck the Congo–Tanzania–Bangweulu Block around 640 Ma.

facts.text: A Snowball Earth glaciation before the Sturtian, about 750 Ma, was once inferred from Kaigas Formation conglomerates on the Kalahari Craton.
The Kaigas Formation proved non-glacial, leaving no evidence for any Neoproterozoic glaciation before the Sturtian.

facts.text: Rifting began as early as 850–800 Ma, perhaps driven by a superplume; most agree the breakup proper began about 750 Ma, with eruptions on most continents.
Rodinia split into Proto-Laurasia, the Congo craton and Proto-Gondwana; new oceans such as the Adamastor and the proto-Pacific Panthalassa opened as Mirovia closed.
By 750 Ma Gondwana had rotated away, leaving Laurentia isolated near the equator; when the breakup ended c. 600 Ma, Baltica became isolated for some 200 million years.
Between 650 and 550 Ma the Iapetus Ocean opened and the Adamastor and Mozambique oceans closed, forming Gondwana.
The breakup may have triggered the Cryogenian Snowball Earth and the rapid evolution of life that followed.

facts.text: Magma flooded more than 1.1 million km² of the Canadian Arctic and northwestern Greenland in about two million years, among Earth's largest magmatic episodes.
U-Pb dating puts its rapid emplacement at about 719.9 and 718.6 Ma.
With the Irkutsk province it marks the rifting of Siberia from Laurentia.
Weathering of its fresh basalt drew down carbon dioxide; glaciation began just 0.9–1.6 million years after its emplacement.

title: Sturtian glaciation

facts.text: A worldwide glaciation lasted from about 717 to 660 Ma, some 57 million years, the first of the Cryogenian's great ice ages.
The longest and most severe known glaciation after the Huronian, it may have been a Snowball Earth with ice at very low latitudes, or several regional glaciations.
Rodinia then lay near the equator, with glacial ice at or below sea level, evidence that the glaciation was global.
Its onset followed the Franklin large igneous province by 0.9–1.6 million years; basalt weathering and low ridge CO2 output after Rodinia's breakup may have caused the cold.
In the snowball episodes ice may have covered all but the highest mountains, with average temperatures about −50 °C.

contested_note: Whether the ice reached the equator (Snowball) or left open water (Slushball) is still debated; the glaciation itself is not disputed.

title: Snowball Earth: the Cryogenian global freezes

facts.text: The Snowball Earth hypothesis holds that Earth's surface froze nearly completely, most commonly linked to the Sturtian and Marinoan glaciations of the Cryogenian.
Glacial deposits formed at tropical latitudes, and glaciers reached sea level near the equator; such deposits are known from every continent.
Whether Earth was a full snowball or a slushball with an open equatorial band of water remains disputed.
Thick ice blocking sunlight would still have severely hindered primary production in shallow seas.
The cooling, and the rapid evolution that followed in the Ediacaran and Cambrian, are thought to have been triggered by Rodinia's breakup.

contested_note: Glaciation itself is accepted, but whether ice covered the whole planet (Snowball) or left open tropical water (Slushball) is disputed.

facts.text: Fossils of testate amoebae (Arcellinida), single-celled organisms with shells, first appear around 700 Ma in the Cryogenian.
Porter (2000) suggests red and green algae, stramenopiles, ciliates and dinoflagellates also evolved during this period.
Fossils of arcellinid testate amoebae date back to the Tonian, around 789-759 million years ago.
Arcellinid testate amoebae are commonly found in soils, leaf litter, peat bogs and in or near fresh water.
Between the Sturtian and Marinoan glaciations came a relatively warm interval with anoxic oceans and rising seas.
Global biodiversity during this interglacial was very low.
Oxygen may have reached about 50% of present levels, though chromium isotopes suggest oxygenation was slow and subdued, a lull in the Neoproterozoic Oxygenation Event.

title: Cadomian orogeny on Gondwana's northern margin

facts.text: As Sturtian glaciers retreated, island arcs began colliding on the margin of future Gondwana, laying down the terranes of Avalonia, Armorica and Iberia.
An Andean-type volcanic arc formed about 650–600 Ma; a back-arc basin opened 590–560 Ma and closed 545–540 Ma.
The Avalonian belt collided with Gondwana around 650 Ma.

title: Algae take over the ocean plankton

facts.text: About 659–645 Ma, red and green algae replaced planktonic cyanobacteria as the main marine phytoplankton, a role they held until the Permian extinction.
Unicellular algae diversified rapidly, and their numbers rose by a factor of one hundred to one thousand.
Late in the Cryogenian, heterotrophic plankton appeared that fed on algae and prokaryotes, ending bacterial dominance of the oceans.

title: First demosponges and disputed Cryogenian sponges

facts.text: Demosponges appear around 650 Ma, building skeletons of spicules from spongin protein and silica.
Some researchers argue the oldest sponge, and so animal, fossils are Cryogenian, but they may be proto-sponges or microbial precursors.
Sponges, which emerged in the Tonian, survived the Cryogenian glaciations.
The oldest sponge spicules, about 580 Ma from China's Doushantuo Formation and Mongolia, are also challenged.
Sponges recognisable as such, such as the non-mineralized Helicolocellus, appear in the latest Ediacaran.

contested_note: The sponge identity of the Cryogenian fossils is uncertain; they may be proto-sponges or microbial structures.

title: Songluo Biota: seaweeds in a Marinoan pause

facts.text: Large macroalgae fossils of the Songluo Biota grew in South China around 650 Ma, during a short break in the Marinoan glaciation.
It is the only known macrofossil biota from the Cryogenian, the first large carbonaceous fossils in rocks of that age.

The Songluo Biota was deposited with no signs of glacial activity, inferred from its shales and siltstones, on a distal shelf likely away from the margins of the large ice sheets of the late Cryogenian.
Macro-algae likely suffered a substantial extinction worldwide during the major glacial periods of the Cryogenian but persisted at less diverse numbers.
The Marinoan, also called the Varanger or Elatina glaciation, was a worldwide glaciation late in the Cryogenian.
Its timing is poorly constrained; a 2025 study dates it to 639–635 Ma.
It is described as the most significant snowball Earth event, global in scope, recorded by diamictites in South Australia's Adelaide Geosyncline.
It ended through volcanic carbon dioxide and dissolving clathrates, perhaps hastened by methane from equatorial permafrost.
It was the last major snowball event; later ice ages covered less of the planet.

title: Cap carbonates seal the last snowball

facts.text: The Ediacaran begins at a cap carbonate, the Nuccaleena Formation, directly above Elatina glacial deposits in South Australia's Flinders Ranges.
Neoproterozoic glacial deposits are commonly topped by a sharply overlying precipitated limestone or dolomite, metres to tens of metres thick.
A favoured explanation: after a snowball, carbon-dioxide-rich acid rain weathered rock, washing calcium into the sea to form carbonate layers.
Their glacial link is questioned: some are too thick for rapid deglaciation, and many glacial sequences lack them.
The boundary also marks the start of a distinctive pattern of carbon-isotope changes.

title: Large ornamented acritarchs replace older plankton

facts.text: At the start of the Ediacaran much of the long-stable acritarch plankton died out, replaced by larger, shorter-lived species.
From 635 to about 575 Ma, large ornamented Ediacaran microfossils, usually over 100 μm across, dominated.
They largely vanish before 560 Ma, about when the Ediacara biota arose; if animal resting stages, they fit frequent Ediacaran anoxia.

facts.text: The Beardmore orogeny built mountains in Antarctica from about 633 to 620 Ma.
It reflects Rodinia's final breakup, as its fragments began moving together again toward Pannotia.
The Beardmore orogeny is expressed as an unconformity in the Transantarctic Mountains, between folded Late Proterozoic strata and overlying Early or Middle Cambrian sediments.
An intracontinental mountain-building event deformed central Australia's Musgrave basement and Amadeus Basin sediments between 630 and 520 Ma.
Its unusual east–west belt suggests India struck Western Australia from the northwest as Gondwana assembled.
It thrust up the rocks that now form Uluru, laid down around 550–530 Ma.

facts.text: Tidal rhythmites, layers of sand and silt laid down off estuaries with strong tides, preserve daily, monthly and seasonal cycles.
Their record fits a day of 21.9 ± 0.4 hours about 620 Ma, with about 400 days and 13.1 lunar months in a year.
Tides slow Earth's spin as the Moon recedes; its average recession since then, 2.17 cm a year, is about half today's rate.

verification.title: Geological constraints on the Precambrian history of Earth's rotation and the Moon's orbit

title: Timanide orogeny on Baltica's northern margin

facts.text: The Timanide orogeny affected the northern Baltic Shield from about 620 to 550 Ma, called the last major orogenic event of the Precambrian.
Around 555 Ma Baltica's northern margin turned active, accreting the Timan-Pechora Basin, the northern Urals and Novaya Zemlya.
Franz Josef Land and Kvitøya most likely became part of Baltica in the Timanide Orogeny.

The basement of Baltica's eastern margin is an Archaean craton and metamorphosed rocks at least 1.6 Ga old, surrounded by the fold belt of the Timanide orogeny and overlain by Mesoproterozoic sediments.

title: Doushantuo Lagerstätte: embryo fossils of Weng'an

facts.text: The Weng'an biota, 609–570 Ma, preserves three-dimensional embryo-like animals in calcium phosphate; its richest layer postdates the Gaskiers glaciation.
The Doushantuo Formation spans about 635–551 Ma, bridging the poorly known time between the Cryogenian and the Avalon explosion.
Caveasphaera, a 609-million-year-old multicellular organism, may record one of the earliest steps in animal evolution.

title: Lantian Biota: early large complex fossils

facts.text: The Lantian Biota of South China, Re–Os dated to 602 ± 7 Ma, holds some of the oldest large, complex fossils known.
It includes macroalgae and putative cnidarian-grade fossils.
Even older macrofossils, the Ancanping assemblage of about 620–610 Ma, occur in the Doushantuo Formation.

facts.text: A mantle plume, the Central Iapetus Magmatic Province, forced Laurentia and Baltica apart, opening the Iapetus Ocean between them.
Rifting began with the Egersund dike swarm in Norway around 650 Ma; from 600 Ma the two continents rotated up to 180°.
The eastern Iapetus opened around 590 Ma, and its southern arm between Laurentia and South America about 550 Ma.
The ocean lasted from about 600 to 425 Ma in the Southern Hemisphere, bordered by Laurentia, Baltica, Avalonia and other continents.
The Tornquist Sea, between Avalonia and Baltica, probably formed at the same time.

facts.text: By about 600 Ma enough oxygen had accumulated to form an ozone layer.
Before this, land-based life probably needed other chemicals to screen out ultraviolet radiation.
Atmospheric oxygen, between 1% and 18% of present levels at 800 Ma, began rising more significantly around 600 Ma.

facts.text: The Pan-African orogeny, a series of major mountain-building events, built the supercontinents Gondwana and Pannotia about 600 Ma.
It began around 635 Ma when the West African and Saharan cratons collided, closing the Pharusian Ocean.
By about 600 Ma most of western Gondwana had joined, while Australia and East Antarctica were still separate.
All African cratons were assembled by about 550 Ma.
Gondwana remained a landmass from about 600 Ma until Pangaea broke up in the Early Jurassic.

title: Pannotia, a short-lived supercontinent

facts.text: Pannotia, also called Greater Gondwana, is a proposed supercontinent that may have formed during the Pan-African orogeny.
It formed around 600 Ma and broke apart only some 50 million years later.
It broke up about 560 Ma as the Iapetus Ocean opened; Laurentia rifted from South America around 565 Ma.
A 2022 paper argues it never fully existed, having begun to break up before it was fully assembled.
Its breakup came with rising seas, dramatic changes in climate and ocean chemistry, and rapid animal diversification.

contested_note: Pannotia's existence is debated; a 2022 paper argues it began breaking up before it was ever fully assembled.

facts.text: A chondritic impactor struck what is now the Gawler Ranges of South Australia about 590 Ma; the age comes from its ejecta in nearby basins.
Estimates of the eroded crater's original size range from 35–40 km to 85–90 km; the larger implies 5.2 million megatons of TNT.
Its ejecta layer, with shocked minerals and an iridium anomaly, lies in Flinders Ranges rocks at least 300 km east.
A radiation of acritarch microorganisms begins just above the ejecta layer, and some authors suspect a link.

title: Earliest widely accepted animal fossils: cnidarians

facts.text: The earliest widely accepted animal fossils are modern-looking cnidarians, possibly about 580 Ma, though the Doushantuo fossils are only roughly dated.
Their presence implies the cnidarian and bilaterian lineages split well over 580 Ma.
Microfossils from 632.5 Ma, just after the Cryogenian ice, may be embryonic resting stages of the earliest known animals.

conflicts.note: Timeline of Earth: first possible corals and anemones

title: Damara orogeny closes the Adamastor Ocean

facts.text: The Damara orogeny sutured the Congo–São Francisco and Río de la Plata cratons 580–550 Ma, forming northern Gondwana with India.
The Adamastor Ocean closed southwards from the Araçuaí Belt to the Kaoko Belt during this time.
In Brazil, the Ribeira Belt collision did most of its deformation 590–563 Ma.

verification.title: A Damara orogen perspective on the assembly of southwestern Gondwana

facts.text: Widespread glacial deposits formed over about 250,000 years, 579.88–579.63 Ma, the last major glacial event of the Proterozoic.
It was the shortest of at least three Neoproterozoic ice ages and, unlike the Sturtian and Marinoan, probably not a Snowball Earth.
Its deposits occur on eight paleocontinents, some at only 10–30° latitude.
It lies just below some of the oldest Ediacaran fossils, though a 9-million-year gap separates them.
A proposed scheme places the base of an Upper Ediacaran series at this glaciation.

verification.title: Dodging snowballs: Geochronology of the Gaskiers glaciation and the first appearance of the Ediacaran biota

title: Avalon explosion: the Ediacaran biota radiates

facts.text: A proposed burst of animal evolution about 575 Ma, named for fossils on Newfoundland's Avalon Peninsula, is thought to have produced the Ediacaran biota.
These large, mostly soft-bodied, often sessile tube- and frond-shaped organisms are the earliest known complex multicellular life.
Metazoan diversity rose quickly, including the first cnidarians and bilaterians, some 36 million years before the Cambrian explosion.
Their place in the tree of life is unclear; it is not even established that most were animals.
Most of these organisms died out in the end-Ediacaran extinction about 539 Ma.

contested_note: The 2008 shape-diversity analysis that defined the Avalon explosion has been disputed; the Ediacaran biota itself is not.

facts.text: The Shuram excursion is a shift in the ratio of carbon-13 to carbon-12 during the Ediacaran, first noticed in South Australia's Wonoka Formation.
Its timing is debated: it began around 573 Ma and ended around 562 or 551 Ma.
It is the largest negative carbon-13 excursion in Earth history, with a 50-million-year recovery, though diagenesis may exaggerate it.
Its cause is unknown; the oxygen-using Ediacaran biota radiated during it, exploiting a surplus of oxidants.
It may have helped spark the rise of animals that led to the Cambrian explosion.

title: Charnia, the first recognised Precambrian fossil

facts.text: Charnia was a frond with leaf-like ridges branching alternately from a zig-zag midline, living on deep sea floors 570–550 Ma.
Found in England's Charnwood Forest, it was the first Precambrian fossil recognized as such.
It is among the most iconic Ediacaran forms, yet among the hardest to place in the tree of life.

facts.text: The first widely accepted burrows come from the lower Blueflower Formation, about 567.3 Ma.
From about 575–560 Ma, mobile organisms left the earliest trails, moving on and just beneath the microbial mats.
These Ediacaran traces are simple, near-horizontal feeding trails.
Bilaterians, animals with bilateral symmetry, were present by 555 Ma.
An animal with leg-like appendages left tracks in mud 551 Ma.

facts.text: Volcanic ash beds date the Mistaken Point fossils to 565 ± 3 Ma and preserve them in fine detail.
It holds one of the most diverse and best-preserved collections of Precambrian fossils.
It defines the deep-water Avalon assemblage, the oldest locality rich in Ediacaran fossils, some of which survive to the Cambrian's base.

title: Unusually weak Ediacaran magnetic field

facts.text: Rocks formed about 565 Ma record an unusually weak geomagnetic field with two distinct directions.
With frequent reversals then, this suggests the solid inner core was only beginning to form, an idea new Cambrian data appear to support.
A 2016 dynamo model predicted a weak field from 1.0 to 0.6 Ga and a strong dipole field after inner-core nucleation.

contested_note: The inner core's age is unresolved, with estimates from 0.5 to 2 billion years; an Ediacaran start is one hypothesis.

title: Earliest possible arthropods

facts.text: The earliest arthropods are placed around 560 Ma.
Ediacaran forms such as Spriggina, Parvancorina and Yilingia have been interpreted as arthropods.
Embryos 543 million years old suggest aspects of arthropod development arose in the late Proterozoic.

contested_note: The arthropod affinity of Ediacaran fossils such as Parvancorina is debated.

title: White Sea assemblage and the Ediacara Hills fauna

facts.text: From 560 to 550 Ma the White Sea biota, named for fossils on Russia's White Sea coast, flourished.
A White Sea bed holds the highest diversity of Ediacaran fossils found, with significant ecological complexity.
South Australia's Ediacara Hills, the period's type locality, preserve abundant fossils of about 555 Ma, like a coeval community in Sonora, Mexico.
Dickinsonia, a large, slow-moving, quilted disc-like proarticulate, first appears about 558 Ma.
Cholesterol found in its fossils in 2018 was taken as evidence it was an early animal, though it may instead point to fungi or red algae.
Its fossils often lie at the end of trails matching its shape, perhaps left while feeding.
Kimberella appears about 555 Ma; some call it mollusc-like, others only a probable bilaterian.
It was almost certainly a triploblastic bilaterian; if mollusc-like, protostomes and deuterostomes split well before 550 Ma.
Scratch marks, perhaps from a radula, and its grazing trail Kimberichnus show it crawled and fed on the sea floor.

facts.text: Several terminal Ediacaran sites in China's Dengying Formation, dated 551–543 Ma, preserve life just before the Phanerozoic.
The Jiangchuan biota is dominated by giant thallophytes but contains fauna similar to later Cambrian sites.
Pyritized fossils at Gaojiashan record how Cloudina tubes grew.

title: Cloudina and the first animal skeletons

facts.text: Cloudinids, an early animal family, lived about 550 Ma and died out at the base of the Cambrian.
Cloudina, Namacalathus and a dozen other organisms built mineralized tubes in carbonate rocks 549–542 Ma.
They are among the earliest and most abundant small shelly fossils with mineralized skeletons.
Cloudina tubes often show predatory borings, so predation was at least present in the Ediacaran.
Rising oxygen lowered ocean acidity and raised seawater calcium around the Ediacaran–Cambrian boundary, possibly prompting skeleton-building.

facts.text: The Proto-Tethys Ocean existed from the latest Ediacaran to the Carboniferous, about 550–330 Ma.
It lay between Baltica and Laurentia to the north and Gondwana to the south.
After the Cadomian events it formed the eastern part of an ocean system subducting beneath Gondwana's northern margin.

title: Transgondwanan Supermountain sheds a vast sediment fan

facts.text: The East African Orogeny raised the Transgondwanan Supermountain, more than 8,000 km long and 1,000 km wide.
Its erosion built the Gondwana Super-fan, over 100 million km³ of sediment laid down over 260 million years.
The flood of sediment coincided with the Cambrian explosion and probably helped early animals diversify.
By the Ordovician the range had been worn down to a plain in modern Ethiopia.

title: Nama assemblage, the last Ediacaran biota

facts.text: The Nama assemblage, the last Ediacaran biotic interval (about 550–539 Ma), was depauperate, never regaining diversity lost as the White Sea biota gave way.
Namibia's Nama Group Lagerstätten preserve Rangea, erniettomorphs and eumetazoans from shallow seas shaped by tides, storms and deltas.
By the end of the Ediacaran, no more than a dozen of 92 possible modes of life were occupied.

facts.text: In the Malagasy orogeny, from the Ediacaran into the Cambrian, India collided with an already joined Azania and Congo–Tanzania–Bangweulu Block.
It affected Madagascar, eastern East Africa and southern India about 550–515 Ma.
The Betsimisaraka suture in eastern Madagascar has been identified as the boundary between the African and India terranes.
The Mozambique Ocean separated the Congo-Tanzania-Bangweulu Block of central Africa from Neoproterozoic India.
The Baykonurian glaciation lasted from around 547 to 540 Ma, late in the Ediacaran.
Its deposits occur in Asia and Africa, and it apparently affected both hemispheres.
It has been proposed as a contributor to the Cambrian explosion.

title: Ediacaran animals evolve longer bodies and keener senses

facts.text: Trace-makers grew steadily more elongate, with bodies over eight times longer than wide by the terminal Ediacaran.
Their trails formed tighter, more accurate loops, and their sensory range grew from millimetres or centimetres to decimetres around 540 Ma.
Some behavioural and sensory innovations of the Cambrian may therefore have begun in the terminal Ediacaran.
The Southern Oklahoma Aulacogen formed between 525 and 550 Ma as Laurentia rifted; its other two arms became spreading zones of the young Iapetus Ocean.
Its flood basalts began or peaked around 540 Ma, covering about 40,000 km² with roughly 250,000 km³ of magma, and are linked to an end-Ediacaran event.
Magmatism came in two phases, first gabbroic and then rhyolitic.

facts.text: The end-Ediacaran extinction, also called the Kotlin Crisis, is a mass extinction near the end of the Ediacaran, the last period of the Proterozoic.
Acritarch diversity fell sharply, and the soft-bodied Ediacaran biota and shelled Cloudina and Namacalathus disappeared.
Both groups vanish abruptly 538.8 ± 0.2 Ma, so their loss cannot simply reflect a closing preservational window.
A major negative carbon-isotope excursion marks the boundary; in Oman it coincides with the last Namacalathus and Cloudina.
Very few organisms crossed the boundary; Cambrian animals then radiated into the vacant niches.
